page.name: Send API
page.h1: A send API your own service can call
page.metaTitle: Send API — send messages from your own application
page.metaDescription: An HTTP API for sending messages from your own service, with per-tenant keys, message status and receipts read back. Channel-scoped endpoints.
page.lede: Product messaging is emitted by code, not typed by a person. The API exists so the service that knows an event happened is the service that sends the message about it.

p: Send endpoints are organized by channel, and the SMS channel is the one with a published reference today. Each channel gets the request shape its transport actually needs rather than one lowest-common-denominator call that fits none of them well.

bullets: Authenticated sends using a per-tenant API key rather than a shared account credential
Message status readable after the send — the acceptance outcome, and the delivery status wherever the provider reports it back
Logs queryable so a support question can be answered from the record

p: There is no idempotency key on the send call, so a retried request sends a second message — duplicate prevention belongs in your caller. And a send is not a transaction: the API returns acceptance, while the outcome arrives later as a receipt. Both are worth designing for before you go live rather than after.

faq.a: The API is HTTP; what a caller needs is the authentication header and the request shape, both documented in the API reference.

faq.q: Can one API key send on every channel?
faq.a: Keys are per tenant, and the send endpoints themselves are channel-scoped — the API reference lists each one with its request shape.

faq.q: Does the API retry a failed send?
faq.a: No. A failed send records its error and the caller decides whether to retry — which is also why idempotency has to live on your side.
